Document trial 1, target length 32768. Read the following document. 1-Flash and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash - for agents that run several sessions, or several people on one PC. - **Everything in the box:** a chat and a live monitor in the browser, pictures on every model, thinking levels, a Models page that downloads, loads and deletes models, a Turbo button, a one-command setup. ## Quick start ```sh git clone https://github.com/mw00/project-maya.git && cd project-maya ./setup.sh ``` The setup asks which model you want, downloads it, builds everything once and **starts the model**. Then open `http://127.0.0.1:8080`. Windows: `START-MAYA.bat` instead of `./setup.sh`. More in [Install](#install). All documentation: [docs/README.md](docs/README.md) ## Pick your model Every Maya quant is named after its model, then its tier - XS, S, M or L, by how many bits its experts keep. The setup recommends one for your PC; to pick one yourself, give its setup id: `./setup.sh --model glm-maya-s24`. | Model | Maya quant · setup id | Size | Made for | | --- | --- | ---: | --- | | **[GLM-5.3-Flash](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash)**

The setup also offers unsloth's GGUF and LibertAIDAI's EXL3 quants of DeepSeek, orcarouter's abliterated DeepSeek, Mia-AiLab's EXL3 quant of MiniMax, turboderp's EXL3 quants of GLM, Qwen-3.8-Flash-Next (CYBER-FROST) as its Q5_K_M GGUF and Qwen-3.8-Flash-Next itself as unsloth's UD-IQ2_XS GGUF, both with pictures ([its settings](docs/SETTINGS.md#qwen-38-flash-next-cyber-frost)). **Each model's files, drafters, pictures and options: [docs/MODELS.md](docs/MODELS.md).** ## Quality Maya's quants are made from each model's released weights and measured against the original: - **GLM-5.3 · Maya quants** keep 97.7-99.2% of the FP8 model's zero-shot accuracy and pick its next token 83-90% of the time (Maya-L: 99.2%, 90%). How they're made and measured: [MAYA-S](bench/results/MAYA-S.md), [MAYA-S24](bench/results/MAYA-S24.md), [MAYA-M](bench/results/MAYA-M.md), [MAYA-L](bench/results/MAYA-L.md). - **DeepSeek V4.1 · Maya-S** picks the same next token as the original 92.6% of the time. - **MiniMax M3.1 · Maya-S** picks it 87.6% of the time (the average over its categories). More on each model's card on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/peasantsmith). ## How fast is it? Real machines measured by our users, most with `./maya.sh --bench` (decode: three greedy 256-token answers; prefill: an 8K-token prompt unless the row says otherwise). Share yours: `--bench`, then `--report`, in a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/mw00/project-maya/issues).

Tool calls are streamed as the model writes them, and a long prompt's reading progress too when a request asks for it (`"return_progress": true`). Coding agents load a server differently, and settings that only matter under that load (`--parallel`, the expert tiers, the batched decode, reading a prompt while others decode, keeping a system prompt for the next conversation) show nothing there. `tools/agent_bench.py` runs a scripted agent workload against a running server, so two settings, two builds or two machines can be compared on the same requests. ## What it sends Everything is fixed by `--seed`, so every run sends the same requests: - `--clients` conversations at once (default 4). Each starts with one of a few shared system prompts (30K, 8K and 4K tokens by default) and a first message of 2-6K tokens. - Then turns: each appends new text, as a tool result or a message would, and asks for an answer of 32-1024 tokens. 80% of the new texts are under 2K tokens, 5% are 8K-64K. The next turn comes 2-20 s after the answer (the agent running its tools). - Checks: at `--checks-per-hour` (40), a 30K-token system prompt with a fresh 2-4K-token question and a 16-token answer, as an agent's permission or routing check does. - Two cold bursts, at a third and two thirds of the run: half the conversations start over and are read again with nothing reusable past the system prompt, as after an agent restarts. - A conversation that grows past `--max-context` starts a new one from its latest turn, as an agent compacts. The model's answers are not fed back: the next turn sends the scripted history, so the prompts do not depend on what the model wrote. Requests are greedy with thinking off and ban the model's end tokens (`--ban auto` knows GLM-5.3-Flash by the served model's name; `--ban none` or token ids otherwise), so every answer writes its whole max_tokens and every run writes the same number of tokens. The texts are slices of this repository's files (`--corpus ` for others). ## Running it Start the server the way you use it (`./maya.sh` with your config, `--parallel` as you run it), then: ``` python tools/agent_bench.py run --url http://127.0.0.1:8080 --clients 4 --label mine --out runs/mine-1.json python tools/agent_bench.py plan --clients 4 # what it would send, without a server ``` A run takes `--duration` (900 s) plus the answers in flight. The first `--warmup` seconds (180) are left out of the summary: the server's caches fill with the conversations then. For an A/B, restart the server before each run (a run leaves its conversations in the server's caches), alternate the settings (A B A B), use the same `--seed`, `--clients`, `--duration` and `--warmup`, and run each setting at least twice: ``` python tools/agent_bench.py compare runs/base-*.json runs/new-*.json ``` `compare` prints each metric's mean and standard deviation over a label's runs and marks a difference larger than twice its standard error with `*`. A difference without the mark is within the runs' own spread. It works against any OpenAI-compatible server (the requests are streamed and timed by the client). A Maya server adds its own figures from `GET /metrics`. ## What it reports Over the window from `--warmup` to `--duration` (a request counts when it ends inside it): | metric | what it is | |---|---| | `output_tok_s` | tokens written per second by all conversations together | | `in_flight` | requests in flight on average (with think times, fewer than `--clients`) | | `decode_median`, `decode_p10` | per request: tokens per second from its first token to its last, what an agent sees; slowed by the other conversations' steps and reads (answers of 50 tokens or more) | | `latency_median`, `latency_p90` | a turn from its send to its last token | | `ttft_median`, `ttft_p90` | a turn's time to its first token: the read of its new text and any wait behind other reads | | `decode K+` | the decode median by the request's context length | | `read +` | prompt reads by their number of new tokens (not reused from the server's cache): new tokens per second of read time - the server's own read time when it sends `timings` (Maya, llama.cpp's server), else the time to the first token | | `vram_hit_per_request`, `vram_hit`, `ram_fetch`, `promo` | Maya with experts in RAM: the routed experts found in VRAM per request (median), and the tiers' readings over the run (VRAM hit, RAM-tier experts fetched over PCIe a token, promotions a token) | The run's JSON keeps every request's times, sizes and the server's records, for anything the summary does not show. ## Reading the results - `output_tok_s` follows the workload as much as the server: with think times, a server twice as fast does not write twice as many tokens, because the conversations wait for their tools. Compare `decode_median` and the latencies for speed; `output_tok_s` and `in_flight` show how the load itself moved. - Reads by new tokens and decode by context length compare like with like when runs drift apart (a faster run gets further into its conversations, so its contexts are longer). - With experts in RAM, runs of the same setting differ more than with every expert in VRAM (where experts end up depends on timing): expect a few percent between reps. # RDNA decode expert kernels For `n_embd=4096`, `n_ff=2048`, the HIP decode dispatcher selects kernels by architecture: | Architecture | IQ2_XXS gate/up (`gate_up<16>`) | IQ2_S down (`down<22>`) | IQ3_XXS down (`down<18>`) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | gfx1100 | Optimized | Optimized | Optimized | | gfx1151 | Optimized | Optimized | Original (legacy) | | gfx1201 | Original (legacy) | Original (legacy) | Original (legacy) | gfx1201 is unchanged and untuned by this expert-kernel work. Other shapes, other quant types, other architectures and CUDA keep the original dispatch. Set `MAYA_HIP_EXPERTS_LEGACY=1` before starting a process to force original HIP expert kernels for an end-to-end comparison. The main change is packed sign expansion: a multiply spreads four sign bits into the high bit of four bytes, then masks and shifts produce the XOR masks and two's-complement corrections. Codebook bytes are positive and nonzero, so ordinary word addition introduces no carries between bytes. This replaces HIP's emulated packed compare/subtract while retaining the original integer scale divisions, FP32 accumulation order, clamping, q8_1 quantization and expert combine order. Gate/up retains sixteen wave32 waves per workgroup, two gate and two up rows per wave, its 2 KiB codebook in LDS, and the fused shared-down branch. Down uses two output rows per workgroup instead of four on optimized paths, reducing its register budget. IQ2_S reads its 8 KiB codebook through global memory; IQ3_XXS keeps its 1 KiB codebook in LDS. The grid selection and sign operations are HIP-only. The signed-codebook technique was adapted from [the upstream engine's moe_fused_iq.cu](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/blob/fb58e0dbc8399662c0e47c76578c6e878b14f6cf/src/prefill/moe_fused_iq.cu) (MIT). Its HIP sign lookup tables were measured first; direct sign arithmetic performed better here. The benchmark retains alternatives for reproducible comparison: sign LUTs, global/LDS codebooks, eight/sixteen gate waves, two/four/eight down rows, alignment-safe eight-byte IQ2_XXS/IQ3_XXS quant loads, a separate shared-down launch, and an eight-wave occupancy constraint. Wider loads, splitting shared down, and the occupancy constraint did not beat the selected paths. This work does not fuse gate/up and down into one kernel. ## Reproduce ```bash cmake -S . -B build-multi -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \ -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/rocm-7.2.1 \ -DCMAKE_HIP_COMPILER=/opt/rocm-7.2.1/llvm/bin/clang++ \ -DMAYA_ENABLE_HIP=ON -DMAYA_ENABLE_CUDA=OFF \ -DMAYA_PREFILL_MMQ=ON -DMAYA_NATIVE_EXPERTS=ON \ -DMAYA_BUILD_TESTS=OFF \ -DMAYA_GGML_DIR=/ai/github/project-maya/third_party/llama.cpp \ '-DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1100;gfx1201;gfx1151' CCACHE_DIR=/tmp/maya-experts-ccache cmake --build build-multi -j 8 \ --target maya hip_expert_kernel_bench glm_ffn_parity glm_layer_parity \ glm_model_test iq1_s_parity hip_intrinsics export HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/rocm/lib build-multi/hip_expert_kernel_bench build-multi/hip_expert_kernel_bench --shared build-multi/hip_expert_kernel_bench --parity-only --sweep build-multi/glm_ffn_parity --selftest build-multi/glm_layer_parity --selftest build-multi/glm_model_test --selftest build-multi/iq1_s_parity build-multi/hip_intrinsics ``` Run these commands from the repository root. `--sweep` also works with timing; without it the benchmark compares original kernels against production dispatch. Baseline launches bypass production dispatch, so both implementations are measured in the same binary. `--shared` includes a Q6_K shared-down matrix of shape 4096x2048 in the gate/up launch and a shared contribution in down. Random finite quantized blocks use the actual GGML block layouts (66, 82 and 98 bytes). Eight expert blobs contain `[gate | up | down]`. Timing rotates five independent pools: each kernel's weight working set exceeds the 7900 XT's 80 MiB cache, including down's smaller matrices. Requested weight and buffer allocations are below 300 MiB for either timed fixture. Parity-only uses one pool and less than 80 MiB. Each timing graph contains sixty launches, with seven alternating original/new rounds after warmup. Reported latency is the median graph time per launch. Setup puts the card with more VRAM first (it takes the bigger first half), leaves the split point to the engine, and writes one hipBLASLt table per architecture (`MAYA_HIPBLASLT_TUNING` takes a path list, `:`-separated on Linux and `;` on Windows; each card uses the table for its own architecture). A discrete GPU paired with a unified-memory APU puts the discrete GPU first and loads the parts sequentially (`MAYA_GLM_PARALLEL_LOAD=0`), so the APU sizes its pool after the first part pins its RAM tier. The two cards may be different architectures. The split passes one small host-memory hop per token, so no peer-to-peer access between the cards is needed. A unified-memory helper reserves slots in the existing portable pinned RAM tier (no second weight copy); a discrete helper uses its own VRAM, automatically sized by aligned expert bytes with 512 MiB left free. Primary admissions, prefetch and background promotions exclude helper-owned experts. At idle boundaries, colder helper experts can be replaced by hotter unowned experts of the same layer. The helper quantizes activations and reduces weighted expert outputs on its GPU before returning one vector per token. CPU quantization runs only for actual CPU fallback; uncovered experts retain the existing CPU/PCIe/disk paths. Batched prefill retains its primary-GPU staging and CPU pool, and may read helper-owned UMA slots without evicting them. All of this is part of the single helper switch; there is no separate optimization flag. Native GGUF experts only; EXL3 is not supported. For physical device 0 = 8060S and 1 = R9700, run the engine with `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1,0`, `MAYA_GLM_EXPERT_HELPER=1` and `MAYA_GLM_SPLIT=0`. The indices are process-local; the system order is unchanged. Keep the normal pack, context, headroom and MTP settings. Unset `MAYA_GLM_EXPERT_HELPER` to restore the existing behavior. This experimental path does not claim general multi-GPU support or a speedup; measure it on the target hardware. #### The helper beside a layer split (two cards and the APU) With `MAYA_GLM_SPLIT=auto` (or pinned boundaries) the helper's device is left out of the split and every part of the split opens its own helper there over its own layers: a part's misses go to the APU, which computes them inside that part's pinned RAM tier at the APU's memory speed instead of the part's CPU lane. On aarch64 the port leaves them out and routes the work through ggml-cpu's own NEON paths: | | x86-64 | aarch64 | | --- | --- | --- | | The Q2_0 pack's expert kernel | AVX-512 VNNI/VBMI | not built: the native packs use ggml-cpu instead | | The EXL3 expert kernels | AVX-512 / AVX2 / scalar | not built: the EXL3 quants do not run (the setup refuses them) | | The native packs (IQ2, IQ3, Q4, ...) | this repository's kernels | ggml-cpu's NEON kernels | | The spin wait | `_mm_pause` | `yield` | | The store fence | `_mm_sfence` | `dmb oshst` | | The CPU feature checks | AVX-512 present or not | always "no AVX-512", so no illegal instruction | `src/kernels/cpu/portable.cpp` replaces the x86 kernels in the build. Its stubs do not silently compute something else: they print what is missing and stop, because a wrong answer is worse than no answer. The canonical Q2_0 pack therefore refuses to start on an ARM CPU with a clear message (`cpu_require_expert_support()`), and the IQ2_XXS pack this setup uses is a native pack - it goes through ggml-cpu. ggml-cpu is built with the CPU's own features, taken from `/proc/cpuinfo`: ``` -march=armv8.6-a+dotprod+i8mm+fp16 ``` The GB10 has `asimddp` and `i8mm`, so the dot-product and the 8-bit integer matrix-multiply paths are on (its `bf16` is not in the string: ggml's ARM backend does not use it). `setup.py` picks the string from the kernel's feature list, so the same setup on an older ARM CPU picks a smaller one. ## The expert pool on a unified-memory device A discrete card reports its own free VRAM, and the pool takes it. A unified-memory device cannot: the runtime's free figure counts the model's file-backed page cache as used (on the test machine it read about 2 GB free with the 90 GB pack cached), so the pool would come out far too small - the start fails with ``` maya generate: glm fast: CUDA0 has no room for the expert pool: 5 slots a layer, at least 8 needed (about 604 MiB more). To make room: a smaller --max-context, --kv int8, or close other programs that use the GPU ``` The pool is therefore sized from `/proc/meminfo`'s `MemAvailable`, which leaves the reclaimable cache out - the kernel evicts it as the experts are read back in: ``` glm fast: CUDA0 unified memory: MemAvailable 99.17 GB, headroom 16.00 GB + 1024 MB reserve, experts need 80.17 GB, pool budget 80.17 GB glm fast: CUDA0 layers [0,45) expert pool 80.17 GB, 288-288 slots/layer (12096 total) glm fast: CUDA0 all experts fit in the GPU pool; RAM tier is staging only ``` - `headroom 16.00 GB` is `MAYA_GLM_RAM_HEADROOM_GB` - the RAM left free for the system (the desktop, the file cache, everything else that is not Maya). Raise it on a busy machine; lower it when the pool is short. - `1024 MB reserve` is the VRAM kept free beside the pool for the driver, the sampler and what is allocated later (a unified device uses 1024 MiB, a discrete card 700). - Nothing is checked after the pool is written: the free figure moves with the page cache, so a second check would give the memory back and then take it away. The start fails only if the pool cannot hold one route's experts in every layer, and it then says how many MiB more it needs. Because the pool is RAM, **other programs on the machine take from it**: the pool is sized from what is free at the start, so a desktop with 40 GB of its own applications running leaves the engine that much less. The RAM tier (the pinned tier below the pool) is staging only when every expert fits, as it does here. The CPU lane - the threads that compute the experts that do not fit in the pool - measures itself against the copy over the link at the start and takes fewer experts when the link is faster: ``` glm fast: CUDA0 CPU lane: 13 threads, an expert 0.171 ms on the CPU vs 0.117 ms over PCIe -> of 0..8 RAM-tier experts the CPU takes 0 0 1 1 1 2 2 3 3 ``` On this machine the link is the faster way, so the CPU lane takes little, and when every expert fits in the pool it takes none at all (`glm fast: CUDA0 CPU lane off: the RAM tier holds no expert`). ## Measured `./maya.sh --bench` with Maya stopped (the standard measurement: three greedy answers of 256 tokens with the thinking off, and a prompt read at 2048 and 8192 tokens).
